These two are completely different, and therefore do not share a single definition. Thus, in order to definitely show the distinct characteristics of each of these two, the division is presented. This division is a division of clarity. By showing the division of clarity, one is able to show the definitive characteristics of each clear aspect; it cannot be done otherwise. Therefore, the division is mentioned solely for the purpose of showing the characteristics. Realizing that it is impossible to show the characteristics without showing the division, the division was stated first. 

If one asks what those two types are: it is stated as "for oneself" <note>Sanskrit: *svārtha*</note>. It is "for oneself" because that by which one understands for oneself is "inference for oneself" <term>svārthānumāna</term> <gloss>inference for oneself</gloss>. "For another" <note>Sanskrit: *parārtha*</note> belongs to the other; that by which another is made to understand is "inference for another" <term>parārthānumāna</term> <gloss>inference for another</gloss>. 

If one asks, among those two types of inference—inference for oneself and inference for another—what is the specific nature of the cognition of inference for oneself? It is stated: "from the triply-characterized sign <note>Sanskrit: *trirūpa-liṅga*</note> in relation to the object of inference." That which possesses the three aspects that will be explained is the "triply-characterized." Because it indicates and demonstrates the meaning by this, it is the "sign" <term>liṅga</term> <gloss>logical sign or reason</gloss>. The statement "the cognition of a person which arises from that triply-characterized sign" specifies it by way of its cause. Because there is also a cognition that arises from the triply-characterized sign and focuses on the triply-characterized sign itself, it is specified by the phrase "in relation to the object of inference." This specifies it by way of its object. The cognition that arises from the triply-characterized sign and focuses on the object of inference is inference for oneself.

Having eliminated misconceptions regarding the definition, in order to eliminate misconceptions regarding the result, it is said: whatever formulation there is of the result of valid cognition <term>pramāṇa-phala</term> <gloss>the fruit or result of valid cognition</gloss>, here in the case of inference as well, it is just like perception <term>pratyakṣa</term> <gloss>direct perception</gloss>. It should be understood in the same way as perception. Just as when one experiences something similar to blue, it is established as blue; likewise here_

<summary>This page explains the division of inference into inference for oneself and inference for another, defining inference for oneself as a cognition arising from a triply-characterized sign in relation to its object, and notes that its epistemological result is established in the same manner as direct perception.</summary>
<keywords>inference, svārthānumāna, parārthānumāna, triply-characterized sign, trirūpa-liṅga, pramāṇa-phala, Buddhist logic</keywords>

The cause of positing <note>the object of comprehension</note>, which is the similarity to the blue, is the instrument of knowledge <term>pramana</term> <gloss>valid cognition</gloss>. Positing this within the nature of comprehending the blue is the fruit of the instrument of knowledge <term>pramanaphala</term> <gloss>the result of valid cognition</gloss>. Similarly, when inference <term>anumana</term> <gloss>logical inference</gloss> also arises in the form of the blue, it posits the comprehension of the blue. Therefore, its similarity to the blue is the instrument of knowledge here, and the very nature of conceptualizing the blue is the fruit of the instrument of knowledge. This nature of conceptualizing the blue is established through the power of similarity, and not otherwise. 

In this way, having cleared away misconceptions regarding number, characteristics, fruit, and the domain of activity in the chapter on direct perception <term>pratyaksha</term> <gloss>sensory or mental perception</gloss>, and having arrived at the proper occasion for the three-fold reason <term>trirupa-linga</term> <gloss>the sign possessing three characteristics</gloss> in connection with that teaching, in order to demonstrate just that, the author states "the three-fold [character] itself" and so forth. What is the three-fold reason? The words "the explanation of this is as follows" are the remainder of the sentence. 

What then are the three aspects? To establish with certainty the presence of the reason in that which is to be inferred <term>anumeya</term> <gloss>the subject of the thesis</gloss>, whose characteristics will be explained, is the first aspect <term>pakshadharmata</term> <gloss>the presence of the reason in the subject</gloss>. Although the word "certainty" <term>nishcaya</term> <gloss>determination</gloss> is not explicitly mentioned here, the final application nevertheless requires those two preceding methods as well. 

Why is this? Because a reason is not a cause for knowing a hidden object merely by way of its suitability, like a seed is for a sprout; for one does not understand fire from smoke that is not perceived. Nor does it illuminate a hidden object by depending on the generation of a cognition that has it as its object, like a lamp does for a jar and so forth; for even if the reason is seen, one does not understand the thesis if the relation <term>vyapti</term> <gloss>pervasion</gloss> is not ascertained. 

Therefore, the function of the reason in understanding a hidden object is solely the certainty of its not occurring without the hidden object <term>avinabhava</term> <gloss>invariable concomitance</gloss>, and it is nothing else. Because the reason is of the nature of an agent, and it must absolutely be ascertained in terms of positive pervasion <term>anvaya</term> <gloss>presence of the reason in similar cases</gloss>, negative pervasion <term>vyatireka</term> <gloss>absence of the reason in dissimilar cases</gloss>, and its presence in the subject <term>pakshadharmata</term>, all three aspects must depend on the word "certainty." Among these, by the word "presence," unestablished reasons <term>asiddha-hetu</term> <gloss>unproven reasons</gloss>, such as "because of being graspable by the eye" <note>when applied to sound</note> and so forth, are excluded.

<summary>This page explains the relationship between the instrument of valid cognition and its fruit using the example of perceiving the color blue. It then transitions to defining the first aspect of the three-fold logical reason, emphasizing that logical necessity must be based on cognitive certainty rather than mere suitability or unperceived relations.</summary>
<keywords>valid cognition, instrument of knowledge, fruit of knowledge, inference, three-fold reason, presence in the subject, certainty, pervasion, Buddhist logic</keywords>

Here in this analysis establishing the definition of logical reasons, the subject <note>the locus of debate, Sanskrit: dharmin</note> is that which is to be inferred. At other times, when the object of proof is being comprehended, the general property <note>Sanskrit: sāmānya</note> is that which is to be inferred. When the pervasion is being ascertained, the property <note>Sanskrit: dharma</note> is that which is to be inferred. To demonstrate this, the term "here" is stated. The subject is so called because it possesses the specific property that one wishes to know, meaning that which one wishes to comprehend.

What is the similar class <note>Sanskrit: sapakṣa</note>? The similar class is that which has a common meaning. By applying the meaning of "similarity" or "resemblance" metaphorically, it is called the similar class, and this is further specified by the term "similar". The similar class is the class that is alike, showing similarity. 

If one asks, "By what is the similar class similar to the subject?"—thinking of what is common to both the subject and the similar class—it is stated: "by the generality of the property to be proven." Because this property to be proven is not yet established, and because a property depends upon another locus, it is the property to be proven. It is not the specific instance that is to be proven, but rather the generality. Therefore, here, the generality is shown to be the object of proof. That is both the property to be proven and the generality. Thus, the meaning is that the similar class is what resembles the subject by way of the generality of the property to be proven.

What is the dissimilar class <note>Sanskrit: vipakṣa</note>? To address this, the text says "the similar class" and explains that whatever is not the similar class is the dissimilar class. What is that which is not the similar class? It is that which is other than the similar class, that which is contradictory to it, and the absence of that similar class. 

As long as one does not know the absence of the essential nature of the subject regarding what is other than and contradictory to the similar class, one cannot comprehend it. Therefore, by the force of conceptualizing them as being other and contradictory, both the other and the contradictory are understood as being of the nature of the absence of the similar class. Thus, the non-existent entity is the nature of the absence of the similar class.

<summary>This text provides a detailed epistemological analysis of the subject, the similar class, and the dissimilar class within Buddhist logic. It explains how these classifications are established based on the generality of the property to be proven and the nature of absence.</summary>
<keywords>logical reason, subject, similar class, dissimilar class, property to be proven, generality, Buddhist logic, epistemology</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>exclusion of existence <note>original: "ཡོད་པ་བསལ་བ་"</note>. In proving that something is produced by effort, impermanence is present in a portion of the dissimilar class <note>original: "མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་"</note> such as lightning, but is absent in other portions such as space. Therefore, this is excluded by the determination.

If the determination is made prior to the term of absence, then the meaning here becomes: whatever is absent in the dissimilar class itself is the reason. If that were the case, then being produced by effort would also be absent in the similar class. Consequently, it would not be a valid reason, which is why it was not formulated in that manner previously.

The determination excludes doubt regarding the reversal from the dissimilar class. If it is taught that "it exists in the similar class itself," is it not already understood that "it is absent in the dissimilar class"? Why then are both formulated? In response: both are grasped to show that only a formulation characterized by a certain positive concomitance <note>original: "རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ་"</note> or reverse concomitance <note>original: "ལྡོག་པ་"</note> should be applied, and not otherwise.

If both of these formulations were indefinite, then the meaning here would be that merely existing in the similar class and being absent in the dissimilar class constitutes the reason. In that case, the reason "because of being his son" in the statement "he is dark-complexioned because he is his son, like the visible son," would incorrectly become a valid reason. Therefore, one must apply only those formulations characterized by certain positive and reverse concomitances through which the connection between the proof-maker <gloss>the reason</gloss> and the object to be proven is realized.

Even when applying them determinately, only one of the two should be applied, not both. Therefore, both are grasped here to instruct that one must apply only that which possesses the certainty of either positive or reverse concomitance. Following the explanation of these three aspects, the objects of inference, the similar class, and the dissimilar class are shown. Hence, their definitions must be stated. What then is the object of inference? It is introduced by the words, "Here, the object of inference is..."

<summary>This page discusses the logical relations of positive and reverse concomitance in Buddhist epistemology, explaining why determination is necessary to define valid reasons and avoid logical fallacies. It concludes by transition to the definitions of the object of inference, the similar class, and the dissimilar class.</summary>
<keywords>Buddhist logic, Pramana, concomitance, similar class, dissimilar class, valid reason, inference</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>is to be projected <note>Tibetan: སྒྲོ་གདགས་པར་བྱ་བ, meaning to impute or superimpose</note>. 

If one asks, "What is that which is suitable to be investigated in such a manner?" It is that which possesses the complete collection of causes for observing its own objective reference. 

If one asks, "When is that collection known to be complete?" It is when another entity, which is merged within a single cognition, is observed. When two entities, which are the objects of apprehension by a single sensory cognition <note>such as the eye sensory power and so forth</note> and are oriented toward what is desired, depend upon one another, they are said to be "merged within a single cognition." When both of these exist, it is not the case that only one is definitely perceived, because there is no difference in both of them being equally suitable for realization. 

Therefore, when one of the entities merged within a single cognition appears, if the other complete collection for seeing also existed, it would definitely be seen. Investigating in this way is the projection of appearance, and its non-observation is the non-observation of the visible <note>Tibetan: སྣང་བ་མི་དམིགས་པ, the non-cognition of an object that is otherwise fit to be perceived</note>. 

Therefore, the very place that is devoid of a flask, and the cognition that observes that place, are called "the non-observation of the visible" because they are the causes for ascertaining the non-observation of the visible. As long as the entity merged within a single cognition is not ascertained, so long is there no certainty regarding the non-observation of the visible. Therefore, the term "non-observation" is also applied to the entity and the cognition. 

The mere absence of seeing is not a means of comprehension because it is itself not ascertained. Therefore, appearance should be viewed as speaking of the place devoid of a flask and the cognition of it as being, by the very force of the words, the nature of the non-observation of the visible. 

If one asks, "What is that which has become the definition of observation?" The text states: "that which has become the definition of observation..." This refers to that which has become the definition of observing a flask. 

"The completeness of other conditions of cognition..." means that the flask produces cognition, and other factors such as the eye are also involved. Whatever cause is other than the visible flask is the "other condition," and their gathering is the "assembly." The nature itself is distinguished from others.

<keywords>non-observation, cognition, visible, flask, sensory power, epistemology, Dignaga, Dharmakirti</keywords>

...is understood as having the nature of elimination. The other two, which are incompatible, are understood by implication <note>original: "shugs kyis"</note> as having the nature of non-existence. Therefore, all three are incompatible classes <note>original: "mi mthun pa'i phyogs", referring to the heterologous class or vipakṣa in Buddhist logic</note>. The statement "the three aspects also possess only three marks" refers to the manner that was already explained. The word "also" <note>original: "yang"</note> is used to include other expressible subjects. 

Others have previously asked about the three aspects and the evidentiary marks that possess these three aspects. The three aspects themselves have already been explained, and the non-cognition <note>original: "mi dམིgs pa", anupalabdhi</note> that possesses these three aspects is now being addressed. The marks possessing these three aspects are also only three. This means there are three types of evidentiary marks possessing the three aspects. 

If one asks what they are, they are: non-cognition possessing the three aspects for proving negation <note>original: "dgag pa bsgrub par bya ba", pratiṣedha-sādhana</note>, and essential identity <note>original: "rang bzhin", svabhāva</note> and effect <note>original: "'bras bu", kārya</note> possessing the three aspects for proving existence <note>original: "yod pa bsgrub par bya ba", vidhi-sādhana</note>. 

To illustrate non-cognition, terms such as "for example" are used. "For example" indicates a demonstration, meaning "just as this non-cognition is presented, so are others, and this is not the only instance." 

A "locality" refers to a specific place. "Distinguished" means particular, referring to the perception of the cognizer. Because this is not the case everywhere, the term "in a certain place" is used. "In a certain place of perception that enables cognition" is the subject <note>original: "chos can", dharmin</note> of the argument. "There is no pot" is the thesis to be proven <note>original: "bsgrub par bya ba", sādhya</note>. 

"Cognition" <note>original: "dmigs pa", upalabdhi</note> means awareness. Its characteristic is the assembly of causes that produce it. Or, it is that which characterizes cognition. The meaning of becoming that is the assembly of causes for its production. The characteristic of cognition is what is called "appearance" <note>original: "snang ba", pratibhāsa</note>. The statement "because of its non-cognition" is the logical reason <note>original: "gtan tshigs", hetu</note>. 

If one asks how something that is absent in a place can appear there, it is said that although it is absent, it is spoken of as appearing there because its appearance is super-imposed <note>original: "sgro btags pa", samāropa</note>. If it were present here, it would certainly be perceived. Therefore, that which is suitable to be evaluated in this way is said to appear, even though it is absent there.

Therefore, the qualified object is that which possesses qualifications. Thus, this qualified nature of things such as a vase, and the aggregation of other conditions, should be understood as forming the definition of apprehension. 

If one asks what kind of qualified nature this is, the text states, "whatever nature exists," and so forth. Apart from the vase which is suitable to appear as the condition of apprehension, if those other conditions exist and are present, then whatever nature becomes directly perceived is the qualified nature. 

The meaning of this is as follows. This definition of direct perception is dependent on a single cognizing subject. When that is the case, and a single observer engages in looking, if the object appears, then both <note>the qualified nature of the object and the necessary conditions</note> are present. If the object does not appear, then because it is obstructed by space, time, or its own essential nature, it is devoid of the qualified nature, even though the other conditions are fully assembled. 

The conditions by which that observer comes to see are nearby. Therefore, those conditions that function for the purpose of seeing are nearby. When one has not engaged in looking, even if the object is in a suitable location, the inability to see it means that it is devoid of the other conditions, although it possesses the qualified nature. What exists far away in space and time is devoid of both. 

In that case, if someone sees something, it cannot be said to be devoid of other conditions, and it is similar to the qualified nature. If one does not see it, what remains in a place where it could be seen is devoid of other conditions, while the other case is described as being devoid of both.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>...is. By using the word "itself," the mistake of being unestablished in one part of the subject is eliminated. For example, in the argument, "Trees have life, because they sleep," where "tree" is made the subject, "sleeping" defined as the folding of leaves is unestablished in one part of the subject. This is because not all trees rely on the folding of leaves at night; it is restricted to only some. 

By placing the word "itself" after the word "exists," the unique property <note>the uncommon or specific attribute</note> is clarified. Indeed, if one merely said "exists in the inferable subject itself," then being audible alone would become a valid reason <note>for proving impermanence, which is over-restricted and does not allow for a general class of evidence</note>. By using the word "certainly," all unestablished reasons that cause doubt are eliminated. 

The definition of the concordant class <note>Sanskrit: sapaksha</note> will be explained below. That the reason is "certainly present in that very concordant class" is the second relation <note>Sanskrit: vipakṣe 'sattva, referring here to the second of the three modes of a valid reason</note>. Here too, by using the word "present," the contradictory reason is eliminated, since a contradictory reason is not present in the concordant class. By using the word "itself" <note>concordant class *itself*</note>, the common indefinite reason is eliminated. This is because a common indefinite reason is not present in the concordant class alone, but what is it then? It is present in both the concordant and discordant classes. 

Placing the restriction <note>itself</note> before the word "present" indicates that even reasons like "arising from effort," which are present but do not pervade the entire concordant class <note>such as impermanent things that do not arise from effort, like lightning</note>, are indeed valid reasons. If the restriction were placed after, the meaning would become: "only that which is present in the concordant class is the reason," in which case "arising from effort" would not be a valid reason <note>for proving impermanence</note>. 

By using the word "certain," the indefinite reason due to doubt regarding the positive concomitance <note>Sanskrit: anvaya</note> is eliminated. For example, in the argument, "Someone is omniscient, because they speak," whether speaking is present in the concordant class of omniscient beings is doubtful. 

The definition of the discordant class <note>Sanskrit: vipaksha</note> will be explained below. That the reason is "certainly absent in that discordant class" is the third relation <note>Sanskrit: trirūpa, the third mode of a valid reason</note>. In this, by using the words "absent in that," the contradictory reason is eliminated, since a contradictory reason is present in the discordant class. By using the word "itself," the reason that is common to a part of the discordant class is eliminated.
